content: Carnauba wax is a natural wax obtained from the leaves of the carnauba palm (Copernicia prunifera), a plant indigenous to northeastern Brazil. It is often referred to as the queen of waxes and is typically found in the form of hard, yellow-brown flakes. The wax is harvested by collecting the leaves of the carnauba palm, beating them to release the wax, and then refining and bleaching the material. Carnauba wax is primarily composed of esters of fatty acids (80-85%), fatty alcohols (10-16%), acids (3-6%), and hydrocarbons (1-3%). Unique to carnauba wax is its content of esterified fatty diols (approximately 20%), hydroxylated fatty acids (around 6%), and cinnamic acid (about 10%). Cinnamic acid, which acts as an antioxidant, may exist in hydroxylated or methoxylated forms. Carnauba wax is widely used for its ability to produce a glossy finish. It is a key ingredient in automobile waxes, shoe polishes, and polishes for instruments, floors, and furniture, especially when combined with beeswax. It is also used as a coating for dental floss. In the United States, its most common application is in paper coatings. Additionally, it is the primary ingredient in surfboard wax, where it is mixed with coconut oil. In the cosmetics industry, carnauba wax is a prominent component in formulations for lipsticks, eyeliners, mascaras, eye shadows, foundations, blushers, skincare products, and sun care preparations. It is also the preferred finish for most briar pipes, as it produces a high-gloss finish when buffed onto wood. Over time, this finish dulls rather than flaking off, as is common with many other finishes. In the food industry, carnauba wax serves as a formulation aid, lubricant, release agent, anti-caking agent, and surface-finishing agent. It is used in baked goods, chewing gum, confections, frostings, fresh fruits and juices, gravies, sauces, processed fruits and juices, soft candies, and products like Tic Tacs and Altoids. It is also employed in the pharmaceutical industry as a tablet-coating agent. Historically, in 1890, Charles Tainter patented the use of carnauba wax on phonograph cylinders as a replacement for a mixture of paraffin and beeswax. When used as a mold release agent, carnauba wax is suitable for applications involving liquid epoxy, epoxy molding compounds (EMC), and certain other types of plastics, unlike silicone or PTFE. It is compatible with epoxies and generally enhances their properties, as well as those of most engineering plastics. An aerosol mold release can be created by suspending carnauba wax in a solvent, and this aerosol version is extensively used in molds for semiconductor devices. Semiconductor manufacturers also use chunks of carnauba wax to break in new epoxy molds or to release plungers when they become stuck. From a technical perspective, the INCI (International Nomenclature of Cosmetic Ingredients) name for carnauba wax is Copernicia Cerifera (carnauba) wax, and its E Number is E903. It has a melting point of 78-85°C, which is among the highest of natural waxes. Carnauba wax is one of the hardest natural waxes, even harder than concrete in its pure form. It is practically insoluble in water, soluble when heated in ethyl acetate and xylene, and nearly insoluble in ethyl alcohol.
